extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, political theory, sociology, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognising and analysing stereotypes, 'codes', and pattern-driven perceptions in public opinion and political argument — what clues indicate false absolutism, selective perception, misuse of space and time, conspiratorial explanation, and dogmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamine visions of the facts (not ideals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful discussion, instead of comparing ideals, reexamines the visions of the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing disputes, examine the different 'visions of the facts' each side assumes rather than debating abstract ideals. Often the parties are working from divergent factual pictures; clarifying and comparing those perceptions leads to useful discussion. (Text example: economic vs patriotic codes seeing different facts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of absolute principles that censor objections
rubrics_metrics.description: When you start to discuss factories, mines, mountains, or political authority as perfect examples of some eternal principle, you are not arguing, you are fighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat invocation of 'eternal' or absolute principles as a red flag: such principles tend to censor objections, isolate issues from context, generate strong emotions, and escalate into further defenses and buffers rather than permitting negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect false absolutism via internal contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are certain clues which often help in detecting the false absolutism of a stereotype: contradictions among the principles invoked are a good clue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for rapidly layered principles that contradict each other (the Ruritanian propaganda used historic right, natural frontiers, reparation, etc.). Mutually incompatible justifications being used together suggests the underlying argument is a stereotype defending itself rather than a coherent factual case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test assumptions of uniform human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that you should do unto others as you would have them do unto you rests on the belief that human nature is uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether arguments depend on an unstated assumption that human nature is the same across contexts. Codes presuppose distinct 'kinds' of human nature; noticing where a code assumes uniformity (or different assumed natures) helps explain why parties see different facts and behave differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify pattern-shaped perception (confirmation bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have the editor's pattern in your mind, you will see vividly the facts that confirm it, vaguely and ineffectively those that contradict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what mental pattern or framework the person is using (e.g., capitalist, socialist). That pattern will make certain facts vivid and will suppress or downplay contradictions. Explicitly name the pattern and test how it selects and weights evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for conspiracy explanations as a stereotype symptom
rubrics_metrics.description: If you go mad looking for plots, you see all strikes, unrest, short skirts, Negro self-assertion, etc., as sub-plots under some grandiose plot engineered by Moscow, Rome, the Freemasons, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sweeping conspiracy interpretations that subsume diverse phenomena as evidence of stereotype-driven reasoning. Such explanations lump unrelated events into a single grand plot instead of analysing independent causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for spatial/practical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Inability to take account of space is another (clue to stereotyping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the claim realistically considers geography, distance, transport and logistics (e.g., the fantasy of projecting a Japanese army 5,000 miles to Poland). Beware reasoning based on map-straight lines or visual imagination that ignores practical means of movement or access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate time-perspective for the issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Time, no less than space, fares badly when it is misconceived; a sound policy must compute appropriate time scales (e.g., forest policy, coal reserves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what temporal horizon the argument employs (specious present, decades, centuries). Misuse of time perspective—treating immediate impressions as decisive for long-run matters or vice versa—distorts judgment. Examples: wills attempting to control too far into future, or ignoring long-term resource limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating concrete facts as eternal principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The very use of these pretentious, absolute principles meant the spirit of accommodation did not prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When actors frame concrete, contingent matters (fact about a mine, port, or factory) as manifestations of an 'eternal principle' (historic right, natural frontier), this abstracts away context and blocks compromise; evaluate whether the principle is being used to obscure empirical trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess vividness versus evidentiary weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Vividness and emotional liveliness can make a preconception seem 'real' and drown out conflicting facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate emotionally vivid anecdotes from representative evidence. Vivid stories may dominate public imagination yet have little evidentiary weight; demand proportionate, generalisable proof rather than relying on striking examples alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate dogma/myth from testable, scientific belief
rubrics_metrics.description: The dogmatist, using a myth, believes himself to share part of the insight of omniscience though he lacks the criteria by which to tell truth from error; the moralist who submits to scientific discipline knows he is in the way of knowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether claims are open to empirical testing and revision (scientific attitude) or are asserted as absolute truths without criteria for refutation (dogma/myth). Prefer hypotheses that can be probed by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect projection of character traits onto groups (stereotyping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'volatile Irishman', 'greedy Jew', '100% American' show early judgements formed long before the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to early, categorical characterizations of groups or persons that substitute stereotype for inquiry. Such projections pre-empt investigation and guide later perception to fit the stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check direction of inference: evidence-first vs theory-first
rubrics_metrics.description: One who generalizes from his knowledge of detail sees further into a generalization than his knowledge extends; conversely, many infer details to fit an accepted generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether conclusions are genuinely drawn from accumulated evidence or whether facts are being picked or stretched to fit a pre-existing theory. Prefer methods that build generalizations from data rather than retrofit data to a favored theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize situational codes within the same person or context
rubrics_metrics.description: A loving father can be a sour boss, an earnest municipal reformer and a rapacious jingo abroad — the same person may operate under different codes in different roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid broad generalizations about 'human nature' based on behaviour in a single sphere. Examine which code (family, business, political) is active in the context and how that shifts perceived facts and appropriate actions.
